## Published Quantitative Evidence on SEM-EDS Accuracy for Aluminum Alloys

### Overview of Available Evidence

Published quantitative evidence on the accuracy of SEM-EDS with silicon drift detectors (SDDs) for aluminum alloys is limited in terms of aluminum-specific benchmarks, but substantial general guidance exists from NIST researchers Newbury and Ritchie, interlaboratory comparisons on related alloys, and multi-technique validation studies.

### General Accuracy Targets from Newbury & Ritchie (NIST)

Newbury and Ritchie have established performance benchmarks for SDD-EDS through extensive validation studies on certified reference materials, stoichiometric compounds, and independently characterized materials (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2). Their 2015 landmark study demonstrated that modern SDD-EDS can achieve accuracy equivalent to wavelength-dispersive spectrometry when following rigorous standards-based k-ratio protocols with proper matrix corrections (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25). The achievable accuracy targets are concentration-dependent: major constituents (>10 wt%) can routinely achieve ±5% relative error, minor constituents (1-10 wt%) approximately ±10% relative error, and trace constituents (0.1-1 wt%) approximately ±25% relative error (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

Their 2024 low-beam-energy study at 5 keV analyzed 263 concentration measurements across 39 elements in 113 materials using NIST DTSA-II software with standards-based k-ratio quantification (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). More than 98% of results fell within ±5% relative deviation from expected value (RDEV), and 82% were within −2% to +2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). For conventional beam energies (≥10 kV), 122 elemental analyses showed all results within ±5% RDEV and 89% within −2% to +2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). These figures represent aggregate performance across diverse materials rather than aluminum-alloy-specific results, but they establish achievable accuracy benchmarks for properly conducted SDD-EDS analysis.

### Interlaboratory Comparisons and Round Robin Studies

An interlaboratory comparison by Jonnard et al. (2015) on a nickel-based metallic glass provides insight into EDS versus WDS performance and interlaboratory variability, though not specific to aluminum matrices (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13, jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). At 15-20 kV, EDS analyses from 57 spectrometers across multiple laboratories showed relative standard deviations of 1.06% for Cr (10.5 wt%), 1.43% for Fe (5.4 wt%), 0.77% for Co (23.5 wt%), 0.40% for Ni (51.4 wt%), and 1.94% for Mo (7.1 wt%) (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13). Mean signed errors relative to reference values were +22% for B, +1% for Cr, −4% for Fe, +0.4% for Co, +2% for Ni, and +6% for Mo (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). WDS showed generally lower dispersion: relative standard deviations of 0.48-1.04% versus 0.40-1.94% for EDS (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13).

At 5 kV, EDS precision degraded substantially, with larger dispersions and mean signed errors of −14% for B, +1% for Cr, −30% for Fe, −3% for Co, +7% for Ni, and −10% for Mo (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). The study demonstrated that low-voltage analyses are more challenging and that WDS generally provides better precision than EDS, though careful EDS implementation can approach WDS performance (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13).

### EDS vs. Alternative Techniques on Aluminum Alloys

Seidel et al. (2021) conducted a comprehensive comparison of EDXRF, WDXRF, LIBS, and spark-OES on commercial aluminum alloys, using spark-OES as the benchmark technique (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 7-8, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 2-4). This study, while not focused on SEM-EDS specifically, provides valuable quantitative data on aluminum alloy analysis accuracy. Three certified aluminum alloy reference materials (EB 313, BAM-311, and EB 315a) were analyzed by spark-OES against certified values (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7).

For EB 315a (an Al-Si-Cu alloy with approximately 9.88 wt% Si, closest to AlSi10Mg among the tested materials), spark-OES showed relative deviations of +1.4% for Si, −0.7% for Fe, +2.7% for Cu, +0.6% for Mn, and +7.5% for Mg compared to certified values (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7). Across the three certified aluminum alloys, spark-OES relative errors were generally below 5% for elements at 1-10 wt% concentration and mostly below 10% for elements below 1 wt% (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7).

For light elements critical to aluminum alloys (Mg, Al, Si), LIBS performed better than XRF techniques due to XRF's lower sensitivity for low-Z elements and absorption by air and detector windows (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). A notable exception was EDXRF measurement of Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7, which showed approximately 2 wt% (about 40% relative) deviation above spark-OES values (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). For most major and minor elements, absolute deviations were below 1 wt% for main components and below 0.25 wt% for minor elements below 2 wt% (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10).

### Standards-Based vs. Standardless Quantification

Newbury and Ritchie strongly recommend standards-based k-ratio protocols over standardless quantification for accurate aluminum alloy analysis (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Standardless normalization (where results are internally normalized to 100%) can conceal analytical problems, particularly specimen topography effects and unmeasured constituents (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6). The standards-based k-ratio method requires measuring standards and unknowns under identical conditions (beam energy, dose, EDS parameters, target orientation, and take-off angle) and applying matrix corrections through software such as NIST DTSA-II (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

For aluminum alloys, suitable standards include pure Al, Si, Mg, Cu, Fe, Mn, and other relevant elements, or stoichiometric compounds for reactive/problematic elements (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). While probably more than 98% of reported EDS analyses use standardless methods, achieving WDS-equivalent accuracy requires the k-ratio/standards protocol with polished standards and unknowns plus rigorous matrix corrections (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

### Effect of Accelerating Voltage

Accelerating voltage significantly affects both spatial resolution and analytical accuracy. Newbury and Ritchie's 5 keV study demonstrated that low beam energy is particularly vulnerable to surface contamination and oxidation effects (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). At 5 keV, surface contamination layers (carbon, oxygen) make the analyzed volume a composite of underlying alloy and surface film, potentially causing significant errors (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). Proper materialographic preparation (mounting, grinding, polishing to <100 nm RMS roughness) is essential, especially for low-energy analysis (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

The 5 kV results from Jonnard et al.'s round robin showed substantially poorer precision and larger systematic errors compared to 15-20 kV measurements (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). For aluminum alloys, 10-20 kV generally provides greater robustness if the relevant X-ray lines (Mg Kα at 1.25 keV, Al Kα at 1.49 keV, Si Kα at 1.74 keV, Cu Kα at 8.05 keV, etc.) remain suitable (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). The beam energy must exceed the critical ionization energy, with efficient excitation requiring E₀ > 2Ec (kallio2025accuracyandprecision pages 15-20, kallio2025accuracyandprecisiona pages 15-20).

### Effect of Count Statistics and Total Counts

Count statistics follow Poisson/Gaussian behavior: one-sigma precision is approximately 3.1% at 1,000 counts, 1.0% at 10,000 counts, 0.31% at 100,000 counts, and 0.10% at 1,000,000 counts (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). These figures describe random uncertainty only; systematic errors from matrix corrections, surface geometry, or detector efficiency remain even with high count totals (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). For trace elements and achieving sub-1000 ppm detection limits, Newbury and Ritchie recommend measurement times of 500 seconds or more to accumulate sufficient counts (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

Higher total counts improve precision but do not eliminate systematic errors from improper surface preparation or unsuitable quantification methods (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 26-29, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). The tradeoff among accelerating voltage, beam current, and acquisition time affects both count statistics and specimen damage/heating (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 26-29).

### Effect of Surface Preparation

Surface condition is critical for accurate aluminum alloy analysis. Rough, scratched, pitted, or oxidized surfaces can substantially alter electron scattering, X-ray generation, and X-ray absorption paths (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6). Newbury and Ritchie emphasize that a flat, highly polished surface below 100 nm RMS roughness is preferable, with <50 nm RMS recommended when analyzing low-energy photons below 1 keV (C, N, O, F, and low-energy L-lines) (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Rough or irregular surfaces produce geometry-related errors that standardless normalization conceals but that remain problematic for standards-based quantification (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6).

Surface oxidation is especially problematic for aluminum alloys at low beam energy, where even thin oxide layers significantly affect the analyzed composition (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). Chemical polishing should be avoided due to potential shallow compositional changes; physical grinding and polishing with fine abrasives (100 nm diamond, alumina, or ceria) are preferred (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Ion beam milling can be used but may implant ions or cause differential sputtering (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Conductive coatings must be applied uniformly to standards and unknowns since thickness differences alter measured intensities (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 29-34).

### Certified Aluminum Alloy Reference Materials

Several certified reference materials (CRMs) suitable for aluminum alloy calibration have been identified, though availability and current certification status should be confirmed with the issuing institutions:

**NIST SRMs**: SRM 85B and SRM 87A are matrix-matched aluminum-base alloy reference materials for Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Mg, Mn, and Cr (yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 3-6). SRM 1258-I and SRM 1259 are Al-alloy spectrometric reference materials used for XRF and atomic emission calibration (yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 3-6). Microscopic homogeneity must be verified before using bulk spectrometric standards for microanalysis applications. Certified compositions should be obtained from current NIST certificates.

**National Institute of Standards, Egypt**: NIS-CRM067 (Si 0.77, Mg 0.71, Cu 2.40, Zn 2.23, Fe 1.56, Mn 0.40 wt%), NIS-CRM068 (Si 0.49, Mg 0.015, Cu 0.59, Zn 0.030, Fe 0.58, Mn 0.84 wt%), and NIS-CRM069 (Si 0.043, Mg 2.17, Cu 1.55, Zn 5.30, Fe 0.12, Mn 0.083 wt%) provide coverage across multiple aluminum alloy families including 7xxx-type compositions (yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 7-9).

**European CRMs**: EB 313 (Al 94.73, Si 0.36, Mg 3.40, Cu 0.093, Fe 0.39, Mn 0.50 wt%), BAM-311 (Al 91.86, Si 0.20, Mg 1.57, Cu 4.65, Fe 0.31, Mn 0.69 wt%), and EB 315a (Al 85.04, Si 9.88, Mg 0.45, Cu 2.46, Fe 0.62, Mn 0.31 wt%) are commercially available certified aluminum alloy references (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7). EB 315a is the closest available CRM to AlSi10Mg composition, though it contains higher Cu and lower Mg than typical AlSi10Mg.

### Specific Findings for Aluminum Alloy Elements

**Magnesium (Mg)**: Light-element analysis (Z=12) is challenging for X-ray fluorescence techniques due to absorption. LIBS performs better than EDXRF or WDXRF for Mg in aluminum matrices (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). One EDXRF measurement showed approximately +40% relative error for Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7 (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). For SEM-EDS at conventional beam energies, Mg Kα (1.25 keV) is readily excited and detected, but surface oxidation can affect results (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18).

**Silicon (Si)**: Silicon analysis shows element-specific challenges across techniques. LIBS agreed better with spark-OES for Si in aluminum alloys than either EDXRF or WDXRF (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). For EB 315a with 9.88 wt% Si, spark-OES showed +1.4% relative deviation from certified value (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7). Si Kα (1.74 keV) is readily analyzed by SDD-EDS at 5-20 kV.

**Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), and Manganese (Mn)**: These transition metals showed generally good accuracy across multiple techniques. Spark-OES deviations from certified values for Cu, Fe, and Mn in certified aluminum alloys were typically below 5-10% relative for concentrations above 0.1 wt% (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 7-8). The Jonnard et al. round robin on a Ni-based alloy (not aluminum) showed EDS relative standard deviations of 1.4% for Fe and interlaboratory mean errors of −4% at 15-20 kV (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13, jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8).

### Open Datasets and Public Data Availability

No dedicated open-access database of EDS spectra from aluminum alloys of certified composition was identified in the published literature. Newbury and Ritchie (2024) mentioned a publicly supported measurement database associated with their study, containing detector configurations, calibration spectra, analyzed material spectra, standard spectra, and Excel files with raw, normalized, and atomic concentrations plus uncertainty budgets (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). However, the excerpt did not provide a public download location or confirm aluminum-alloy coverage.

The NIST DTSA-II software and source code are publicly available (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4), providing the quantification engine used in the Newbury and Ritchie studies. This software implements standards-based k-ratio protocols with comprehensive matrix corrections and uncertainty budgets, making it valuable for reproducing and validating quantitative aluminum alloy measurements even in the absence of a dedicated spectral database (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

### Recommendations for AlSi10Mg Calibration

For calibrating quantitative SEM-EDS on LPBF AlSi10Mg powder and printed parts:

1. **Standards-based protocol**: Use pure Al, Si, and Mg metal standards, or suitable compounds for elements difficult to handle in pure form. Measure k-ratios following the protocol described by Goldstein et al. and Newbury & Ritchie, implementing NIST DTSA-II for matrix corrections (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

2. **Certified reference materials**: EB 315a (9.88 wt% Si, 0.45 wt% Mg, 2.46 wt% Cu) is the closest available CRM to AlSi10Mg, though Cu content differs. NIS-CRM067, NIS-CRM068, NIS-CRM069, or NIST SRM 85B/87A may provide suitable matrix-matched materials for method validation (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 7-9, yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 3-6).

3. **Surface preparation**: Polish samples to <100 nm RMS roughness using physical abrasives. Avoid chemical polishing. For LPBF powder, embedding and polishing cross-sections is preferable to analyzing irregular particle surfaces (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

4. **Beam energy**: Use 15 or 20 kV for robust analysis of Al, Si, Mg, and typical minor elements (Fe, Mn, Cu). Lower voltages (5-10 kV) improve spatial resolution but increase vulnerability to surface contamination (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18).

5. **Count statistics**: Acquire sufficient counts for desired precision: 10,000+ counts for 1% precision on major peaks, 100,000+ for 0.3% precision (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). For minor elements (0.2-0.5 wt% Mg), 500-second or longer acquisition times may be needed (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

6. **Independent validation**: Compare SEM-EDS results against spark-OES, LIBS, or ICP-OES measurements on the same samples. Spark-OES typically achieves <10% relative error for elements >0.1 wt% in aluminum alloys (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 7-8). Alternatively, WDS/EPMA provides higher-precision independent measurements for validation (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13).

### Limitations and Gaps in Published Evidence

The published literature contains limited aluminum-alloy-specific quantitative SEM-EDS validation data, particularly for:
- LPBF AlSi10Mg and other additive manufacturing aluminum alloys
- 7xxx-series, Al-Cu-Li, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Zr-Er-Sc, and other specialized alloy families mentioned
- Direct element-by-element EDS accuracy benchmarks for Mg, Si, Cu, Zn, Fe, and Mn in aluminum matrices versus certified compositions
- Open-access EDS spectral databases from certified aluminum alloys

Most quantitative evidence comes from general SDD-EDS validation studies (not aluminum-specific) or comparisons using alternative techniques (XRF, LIBS, spark-OES) rather than SEM-EDS directly. The interlaboratory round robins identified involved Ni-based metallic glass rather than aluminum alloys. These gaps suggest opportunities for future work to establish rigorous aluminum-alloy-specific EDS benchmarks, particularly for the alloy families relevant to additive manufacturing and advanced aerospace/automotive applications.

### General Accuracy Targets from Newbury & Ritchie (NIST)

Newbury and Ritchie have established performance benchmarks for SDD-EDS through extensive validation studies on certified reference materials, stoichiometric compounds, and independently characterized materials (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000028). Their 2015 landmark study demonstrated that modern SDD-EDS can achieve accuracy equivalent to wavelength-dispersive spectrometry when following rigorous standards-based k-ratio protocols with proper matrix corrections (pqac-00000000). The achievable accuracy targets are concentration-dependent: major constituents (>10 wt%) can routinely achieve ±5% relative error, minor constituents (1-10 wt%) approximately ±10% relative error, and trace constituents (0.1-1 wt%) approximately ±25% relative error (pqac-00000000).

Their 2024 low-beam-energy study at 5 keV analyzed 263 concentration measurements across 39 elements in 113 materials using NIST DTSA-II software with standards-based k-ratio quantification (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000027). More than 98% of results fell within ±5% relative deviation from expected value (RDEV), and 82% were within −2% to +2% RDEV (pqac-00000001). For conventional beam energies (≥10 kV), 122 elemental analyses showed all results within ±5% RDEV and 89% within −2% to +2% RDEV (pqac-00000001). These figures represent aggregate performance across diverse materials rather than aluminum-alloy-specific results, but they establish achievable accuracy benchmarks for properly conducted SDD-EDS analysis.

### Interlaboratory Comparisons and Round Robin Studies

An interlaboratory comparison by Jonnard et al. (2015) on a nickel-based metallic glass provides insight into EDS versus WDS performance and interlaboratory variability, though not specific to aluminum matrices (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008). At 15-20 kV, EDS analyses from 57 spectrometers across multiple laboratories showed relative standard deviations of 1.06% for Cr (10.5 wt%), 1.43% for Fe (5.4 wt%), 0.77% for Co (23.5 wt%), 0.40% for Ni (51.4 wt%), and 1.94% for Mo (7.1 wt%) (pqac-00000002). Mean signed errors relative to reference values were +22% for B, +1% for Cr, −4% for Fe, +0.4% for Co, +2% for Ni, and +6% for Mo (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008). WDS showed generally lower dispersion: relative standard deviations of 0.48-1.04% versus 0.40-1.94% for EDS (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006).

At 5 kV, EDS precision degraded substantially, with larger dispersions and mean signed errors of −14% for B, +1% for Cr, −30% for Fe, −3% for Co, +7% for Ni, and −10% for Mo (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008). The study demonstrated that low-voltage analyses are more challenging and that WDS generally provides better precision than EDS, though careful EDS implementation can approach WDS performance (pqac-00000006).

### EDS vs. Alternative Techniques on Aluminum Alloys

Seidel et al. (2021) conducted a comprehensive comparison of EDXRF, WDXRF, LIBS, and spark-OES on commercial aluminum alloys, using spark-OES as the benchmark technique (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013). This study, while not focused on SEM-EDS specifically, provides valuable quantitative data on aluminum alloy analysis accuracy. Three certified aluminum alloy reference materials (EB 313, BAM-311, and EB 315a) were analyzed by spark-OES against certified values (pqac-00000009).

For EB 315a (an Al-Si-Cu alloy with approximately 9.88 wt% Si, closest to AlSi10Mg among the tested materials), spark-OES showed relative deviations of +1.4% for Si, −0.7% for Fe, +2.7% for Cu, +0.6% for Mn, and +7.5% for Mg compared to certified values (pqac-00000009). Across the three certified aluminum alloys, spark-OES relative errors were generally below 5% for elements at 1-10 wt% concentration and mostly below 10% for elements below 1 wt% (pqac-00000009).

For light elements critical to aluminum alloys (Mg, Al, Si), LIBS performed better than XRF techniques due to XRF's lower sensitivity for low-Z elements and absorption by air and detector windows (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012). A notable exception was EDXRF measurement of Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7, which showed approximately 2 wt% (about 40% relative) deviation above spark-OES values (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012). For most major and minor elements, absolute deviations were below 1 wt% for main components and below 0.25 wt% for minor elements below 2 wt% (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000012).

### Standards-Based vs. Standardless Quantification

Newbury and Ritchie strongly recommend standards-based k-ratio protocols over standardless quantification for accurate aluminum alloy analysis (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). Standardless normalization (where results are internally normalized to 100%) can conceal analytical problems, particularly specimen topography effects and unmeasured constituents (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000021). The standards-based k-ratio method requires measuring standards and unknowns under identical conditions (beam energy, dose, EDS parameters, target orientation, and take-off angle) and applying matrix corrections through software such as NIST DTSA-II (pqac-00000029).

For aluminum alloys, suitable standards include pure Al, Si, Mg, Cu, Fe, Mn, and other relevant elements, or stoichiometric compounds for reactive/problematic elements (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). While probably more than 98% of reported EDS analyses use standardless methods, achieving WDS-equivalent accuracy requires the k-ratio/standards protocol with polished standards and unknowns plus rigorous matrix corrections (pqac-00000000).

### Effect of Accelerating Voltage

Accelerating voltage significantly affects both spatial resolution and analytical accuracy. Newbury and Ritchie's 5 keV study demonstrated that low beam energy is particularly vulnerable to surface contamination and oxidation effects (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000024). At 5 keV, surface contamination layers (carbon, oxygen) make the analyzed volume a composite of underlying alloy and surface film, potentially causing significant errors (pqac-00000017). Proper materialographic preparation (mounting, grinding, polishing to <100 nm RMS roughness) is essential, especially for low-energy analysis (pqac-00000029).

The 5 kV results from Jonnard et al.'s round robin showed substantially poorer precision and larger systematic errors compared to 15-20 kV measurements (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008). For aluminum alloys, 10-20 kV generally provides greater robustness if the relevant X-ray lines (Mg Kα at 1.25 keV, Al Kα at 1.49 keV, Si Kα at 1.74 keV, Cu Kα at 8.05 keV, etc.) remain suitable (pqac-00000017). The beam energy must exceed the critical ionization energy, with efficient excitation requiring E₀ > 2Ec (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016).

### Effect of Count Statistics and Total Counts

Count statistics follow Poisson/Gaussian behavior: one-sigma precision is approximately 3.1% at 1,000 counts, 1.0% at 10,000 counts, 0.31% at 100,000 counts, and 0.10% at 1,000,000 counts (pqac-00000019). These figures describe random uncertainty only; systematic errors from matrix corrections, surface geometry, or detector efficiency remain even with high count totals (pqac-00000019). For trace elements and achieving sub-1000 ppm detection limits, Newbury and Ritchie recommend measurement times of 500 seconds or more to accumulate sufficient counts (pqac-00000000).

Higher total counts improve precision but do not eliminate systematic errors from improper surface preparation or unsuitable quantification methods (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019). The tradeoff among accelerating voltage, beam current, and acquisition time affects both count statistics and specimen damage/heating (pqac-00000014).

### Effect of Surface Preparation

Surface condition is critical for accurate aluminum alloy analysis. Rough, scratched, pitted, or oxidized surfaces can substantially alter electron scattering, X-ray generation, and X-ray absorption paths (pqac-00000021). Newbury and Ritchie emphasize that a flat, highly polished surface below 100 nm RMS roughness is preferable, with <50 nm RMS recommended when analyzing low-energy photons below 1 keV (C, N, O, F, and low-energy L-lines) (pqac-00000029). Rough or irregular surfaces produce geometry-related errors that standardless normalization conceals but that remain problematic for standards-based quantification (pqac-00000021).

Surface oxidation is especially problematic for aluminum alloys at low beam energy, where even thin oxide layers significantly affect the analyzed composition (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000024). Chemical polishing should be avoided due to potential shallow compositional changes; physical grinding and polishing with fine abrasives (100 nm diamond, alumina, or ceria) are preferred (pqac-00000029). Ion beam milling can be used but may implant ions or cause differential sputtering (pqac-00000029). Conductive coatings must be applied uniformly to standards and unknowns since thickness differences alter measured intensities (pqac-00000020).

### Certified Aluminum Alloy Reference Materials

Several certified reference materials (CRMs) suitable for aluminum alloy calibration have been identified, though availability and current certification status should be confirmed with the issuing institutions:

**NIST SRMs**: SRM 85B and SRM 87A are matrix-matched aluminum-base alloy reference materials for Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Mg, Mn, and Cr (pqac-00000023). SRM 1258-I and SRM 1259 are Al-alloy spectrometric reference materials used for XRF and atomic emission calibration (pqac-00000023). Microscopic homogeneity must be verified before using bulk spectrometric standards for microanalysis applications. Certified compositions should be obtained from current NIST certificates.

**National Institute of Standards, Egypt**: NIS-CRM067 (Si 0.77, Mg 0.71, Cu 2.40, Zn 2.23, Fe 1.56, Mn 0.40 wt%), NIS-CRM068 (Si 0.49, Mg 0.015, Cu 0.59, Zn 0.030, Fe 0.58, Mn 0.84 wt%), and NIS-CRM069 (Si 0.043, Mg 2.17, Cu 1.55, Zn 5.30, Fe 0.12, Mn 0.083 wt%) provide coverage across multiple aluminum alloy families including 7xxx-type compositions (pqac-00000022).

**European CRMs**: EB 313 (Al 94.73, Si 0.36, Mg 3.40, Cu 0.093, Fe 0.39, Mn 0.50 wt%), BAM-311 (Al 91.86, Si 0.20, Mg 1.57, Cu 4.65, Fe 0.31, Mn 0.69 wt%), and EB 315a (Al 85.04, Si 9.88, Mg 0.45, Cu 2.46, Fe 0.62, Mn 0.31 wt%) are commercially available certified aluminum alloy references (pqac-00000009). EB 315a is the closest available CRM to AlSi10Mg composition, though it contains higher Cu and lower Mg than typical AlSi10Mg.

### Specific Findings for Aluminum Alloy Elements

**Magnesium (Mg)**: Light-element analysis (Z=12) is challenging for X-ray fluorescence techniques due to absorption. LIBS performs better than EDXRF or WDXRF for Mg in aluminum matrices (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012). One EDXRF measurement showed approximately +40% relative error for Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7 (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012). For SEM-EDS at conventional beam energies, Mg Kα (1.25 keV) is readily excited and detected, but surface oxidation can affect results (pqac-00000017).

**Silicon (Si)**: Silicon analysis shows element-specific challenges across techniques. LIBS agreed better with spark-OES for Si in aluminum alloys than either EDXRF or WDXRF (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000012). For EB 315a with 9.88 wt% Si, spark-OES showed +1.4% relative deviation from certified value (pqac-00000009). Si Kα (1.74 keV) is readily analyzed by SDD-EDS at 5-20 kV.

**Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), and Manganese (Mn)**: These transition metals showed generally good accuracy across multiple techniques. Spark-OES deviations from certified values for Cu, Fe, and Mn in certified aluminum alloys were typically below 5-10% relative for concentrations above 0.1 wt% (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). The Jonnard et al. round robin on a Ni-based alloy (not aluminum) showed EDS relative standard deviations of 1.4% for Fe and interlaboratory mean errors of −4% at 15-20 kV (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003).

### Open Datasets and Public Data Availability

No dedicated open-access database of EDS spectra from aluminum alloys of certified composition was identified in the published literature. Newbury and Ritchie (2024) mentioned a publicly supported measurement database associated with their study, containing detector configurations, calibration spectra, analyzed material spectra, standard spectra, and Excel files with raw, normalized, and atomic concentrations plus uncertainty budgets (pqac-00000024). However, the excerpt did not provide a public download location or confirm aluminum-alloy coverage.

The NIST DTSA-II software and source code are publicly available (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029), providing the quantification engine used in the Newbury and Ritchie studies. This software implements standards-based k-ratio protocols with comprehensive matrix corrections and uncertainty budgets, making it valuable for reproducing and validating quantitative aluminum alloy measurements even in the absence of a dedicated spectral database (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000029).

### Recommendations for AlSi10Mg Calibration

For calibrating quantitative SEM-EDS on LPBF AlSi10Mg powder and printed parts:

1. **Standards-based protocol**: Use pure Al, Si, and Mg metal standards, or suitable compounds for elements difficult to handle in pure form. Measure k-ratios following the protocol described by Goldstein et al. and Newbury & Ritchie, implementing NIST DTSA-II for matrix corrections (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029).

2. **Certified reference materials**: EB 315a (9.88 wt% Si, 0.45 wt% Mg, 2.46 wt% Cu) is the closest available CRM to AlSi10Mg, though Cu content differs. NIS-CRM067, NIS-CRM068, NIS-CRM069, or NIST SRM 85B/87A may provide suitable matrix-matched materials for method validation (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023).

3. **Surface preparation**: Polish samples to <100 nm RMS roughness using physical abrasives. Avoid chemical polishing. For LPBF powder, embedding and polishing cross-sections is preferable to analyzing irregular particle surfaces (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000029).

4. **Beam energy**: Use 15 or 20 kV for robust analysis of Al, Si, Mg, and typical minor elements (Fe, Mn, Cu). Lower voltages (5-10 kV) improve spatial resolution but increase vulnerability to surface contamination (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000017).

5. **Count statistics**: Acquire sufficient counts for desired precision: 10,000+ counts for 1% precision on major peaks, 100,000+ for 0.3% precision (pqac-00000019). For minor elements (0.2-0.5 wt% Mg), 500-second or longer acquisition times may be needed (pqac-00000000).

6. **Independent validation**: Compare SEM-EDS results against spark-OES, LIBS, or ICP-OES measurements on the same samples. Spark-OES typically achieves <10% relative error for elements >0.1 wt% in aluminum alloys (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). Alternatively, WDS/EPMA provides higher-precision independent measurements for validation (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006).

### Limitations and Gaps in Published Evidence

The published literature contains limited aluminum-alloy-specific quantitative SEM-EDS validation data, particularly for:
- LPBF AlSi10Mg and other additive manufacturing aluminum alloys
- 7xxx-series, Al-Cu-Li, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Zr-Er-Sc, and other specialized alloy families mentioned
- Direct element-by-element EDS accuracy benchmarks for Mg, Si, Cu, Zn, Fe, and Mn in aluminum matrices versus certified compositions
- Open-access EDS spectral databases from certified aluminum alloys

Most quantitative evidence comes from general SDD-EDS validation studies (not aluminum-specific) or comparisons using alternative techniques (XRF, LIBS, spark-OES) rather than SEM-EDS directly. The interlaboratory round robins identified involved Ni-based metallic glass rather than aluminum alloys. These gaps suggest opportunities for future work to establish rigorous aluminum-alloy-specific EDS benchmarks, particularly for the alloy families relevant to additive manufacturing and advanced aerospace/automotive applications.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides aggregate RDEV performance rather than aluminum-alloy-specific values. For 263 concentration measurements covering 39 elements in 113 materials analyzed at E0 = 5 keV with DTSA-II, more than 98% of atomic-concentration results were within ±5% RDEV, and 82% were within −2% to +2% RDEV. The subset involving characteristic X-ray energies from 0–1.5 keV and the subset from 1.5–5 keV had similar RDEV distributions. A separate conventional-analysis comparison, using E0 ≥ 10 keV and augmented with additional II-VI and II-V compounds, included 122 elemental analyses: all results were within ±5% RDEV and 89% were within −2% to +2% RDEV. For several metal alloys lacking independent reference analyses, the 5 keV expected values were based on concentrations measured at E0 = 20 keV using higher-energy characteristic lines. contexts.context: The excerpt reports a comparative study of commercial aluminum and steel alloys using EDXRF, WDXRF, LIBS, and spark-OES, with spark-OES treated as the benchmark. It does not describe an interlaboratory comparison or formal round-robin study, and it does not discuss EDS specifically; EDXRF is the X-ray method examined. Across most major and minor elements, EDXRF, WDXRF, and LIBS showed small absolute deviations from spark-OES, generally in the low wt.% range. However, relative errors could exceed 100% when concentrations were below 1 wt.%, because precision and detection-limit effects become important. A notable aluminum-alloy exception was magnesium in AlMg4.5Mn0.7, for which EDXRF was approximately 2 wt.%—about 40% relative to the detected concentration—above spark-OES. For light elements such as Mg, Al, and Si in aluminum matrices, LIBS performed better than the X-ray techniques. LIBS generally agreed well with spark-OES but showed deviations exceeding 35% for some measurements in high-alloyed steel. The study emphasizes that accuracy depends on element, matrix, concentration range, calibration, and application; it does not provide interlaboratory precision statistics such as repeatability or reproducibility standard deviations.
contexts.question: What interlaboratory comparison or round robin studies on EDS analysis of aluminum alloys or metal alloys have been conducted, and what were the measured accuracy or precision values for different elements?

Reported repeatability/reproducibility values were below 0.11% RSD for pure Au, 0.16% RSD for Au-Ag and Au-Ag-Cu mixtures, and below 0.20% RSD for Au-Ag-Cu mixtures. Without correction, the corresponding RSD values were 0.16%, 0.23%, 0.22%, and 0.27%, respectively. contexts.context: The excerpt reports an interlaboratory comparison of quantitative EDS on a metallic glass alloy, rather than an aluminum alloy specifically. At 15–20 kV, 57 spectrometers produced 64 analyses. The reference mass fractions (wt%) were B 3.6, Cr 10.4, Fe 5.6, Co 23.4, Ni 50.3, and Mo 6.7. Corresponding measured means ± standard deviations were B 4.4 ± 3.0, Cr 10.5 ± 0.6, Fe 5.4 ± 0.4, Co 23.5 ± 0.8, Ni 51.4 ± 2.1, and Mo 7.1 ± 1.4. The full measurement ranges were B 1.2–10.6, Cr 9.1–12.5, Fe 2.9–5.9, Co 21.3–25.3, Ni 45.4–56.9, and Mo 4.2–14.1 wt%. At 5 kV, 43 analyses were conducted; means ± standard deviations were B 3.1 ± 2.0, Cr 10.5 ± 3.8, Fe 3.9 ± 2.8, Co 22.8 ± 5.3, Ni 54.0 ± 4.7, and Mo 6.0 ± 1.9 wt%, with substantially wider ranges. The study found generally reasonable agreement with reference values, but poorer precision at 5 kV. Numerical-filter background subtraction improved accuracy and reduced dispersion compared with modeled backgrounds. Aluminum was detected or treated in only 28 of the higher-voltage analyses, but no separate aluminum accuracy values are provided in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report measurements specifically labeled EDS or EPMA; it compares EDXRF and WDXRF with LIBS against spark-OES benchmarks. For aluminum alloy compositions, the main-element results (including Al) generally agreed well: absolute deviations for Al, Fe, and Cu were below 1 wt.%, while minor elements below 2 wt.% differed by less than 0.25 wt.% in absolute terms. Relative deviations were generally below 3% for main components, but were higher for side elements, particularly Si in aluminum alloys. A notable aluminum-alloy exception was AlMg4.5Mn, for which the EDXRF aluminum result showed a significant mismatch, although the excerpt does not give its numerical error. For Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7, EDXRF measured approximately 2 wt.% more than spark-OES, corresponding to about a 40% relative error. The Al99.5 alloy showed an extreme relative discrepancy for EDXRF: 0.196 wt.% compared with 0.004 wt.% by spark-OES, or approximately 5000% relative deviation; this was a large percentage error on a very small absolute concentration. The excerpt also states that LIBS gave better Si agreement than either XRF method.

Three aluminum certified reference alloys were compared with spark-OES: EB 313, BAM-311, and EB 315a. The reported columns are Al, Si, Fe, Cu, Mn, Mg, Cr, and Ni. For BAM-311, Al was 91.861 versus 91.597%, Si 0.204 versus 0.2077%, Fe 0.310 versus 0.3186%, Cu 4.653 versus 4.801%, Mn 0.694 versus 0.668%, and Mg 1.567 versus 1.642%. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that surface condition and accelerating voltage can strongly affect EDS accuracy, whereas it provides less direct evidence about total counts or polished-versus-rough aluminum alloys specifically. Surface oxidation or other atmospheric reaction layers are especially important at low beam energy: they make the analyzed volume a composite of the underlying alloy and surface film, potentially causing significant errors. The authors therefore screened spectra as a function of beam energy; increasing C and O signals at reduced voltage were used to identify and reject unsuitable materials. Proper materialographic preparation (mounting, grinding, and polishing) was used, and homogeneity was checked by point-beam sampling, suggesting that a polished, clean, homogeneous surface is preferred over a rough or contaminated one. The examples compare 5, 10, and 15–20 kV: contaminated AlN showed increasing C/O contributions as voltage decreased, while an acceptable Au-Cu standard showed only a small relative increase. Thus, for aluminum alloys, 5 kV is more vulnerable to surface-film and contamination effects, while 10–20 kV generally provides greater robustness if the relevant X-ray lines remain suitable. The excerpt states that uncertainty includes measurement statistics from both sample and standard, implying that higher total counts reduce statistical uncertainty, but it does not quantify the count dependence or establish a specific optimum.

Regarding total counts, increasing SEM beam intensity produced more than a tenfold increase in integral counts. This was accompanied by an increase in detector dead time from 1% to 6–20%, indicating that higher counts can alter acquisition conditions and potentially affect quantitative accuracy if dead-time effects are not controlled. contexts.context: The excerpt provides EPMA information that is broadly applicable to EDS aluminum-alloy analysis. Higher total counts, achieved through longer count times or higher beam current, improve analytical sensitivity and counting precision, while background counts must be distinguished from characteristic X-ray counts. The listed example gives an aluminum Kα detection limit of about 20 ppm in quartz at 20 kV, 100 nA, and 640 s, illustrating the tradeoff among voltage, current, and acquisition time. Count statistics are therefore central to accuracy: insufficient net counts increase uncertainty and detection limits, whereas more counts generally improve precision, provided beam damage and instrumental artifacts remain controlled. Accelerating voltage affects X-ray generation and beam heating. The excerpt’s aluminum example uses 20 kV, while its heating discussion shows that temperature rise depends on beam energy, current, thermal conductivity, and beam diameter; low-conductivity materials can experience substantial heating. Surface preparation is not discussed directly in terms of polished versus rough surfaces. However, the text warns that sample geometry and inhomogeneity affect matrix corrections: measurements spanning interfaces or nonuniform regions can yield incorrect ZAF/φ(ρz) corrections if treated as a homogeneous alloy. Thus, a smooth, well-polished, homogeneous surface would generally better support reliable quantification, although that conclusion is inferred rather than explicitly stated here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides information mainly applicable to the counting-statistics and accelerating-voltage aspects of EDS accuracy. Increasing total counts by collecting longer or using higher count rates reduces statistical uncertainty: approximately 3.1% precision is associated with 1,000 counts, 1% with 10,000, 0.31% with 100,000, and 0.1% with 1,000,000 counts, assuming Gaussian statistics. At low count rates, Poisson statistics are more appropriate, while higher count rates approach Gaussian behavior. These figures describe precision rather than total accuracy; systematic errors can remain even with very large count totals. Accuracy is also constrained by matrix corrections, including atomic-number, absorption, and fluorescence effects, particularly when the reference standard and aluminum-alloy unknown differ in composition. Accelerating voltage is identified as an important correction parameter, along with takeoff angle and mass absorption coefficients. The excerpt does not discuss polished versus rough surfaces, so it provides no direct evidence about surface preparation. It also does not quantify the effect of operating specifically between 5 and 20 kV; it only indicates that electron energy affects x-ray generation and correction behavior. Thus, voltage changes should be evaluated alongside excitation conditions and matrix corrections rather than inferred solely from count statistics.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative guidance for evaluating EDS accuracy in aluminum alloys but does not give numerical results specifically linking total counts, count statistics, or 5–20 kV settings to aluminum-alloy errors. EDS derives qualitative information from X-ray energy and quantitative information from peak intensity; therefore, increasing total counts generally improves counting statistics and reduces random uncertainty, although this relationship is not explicitly discussed in the excerpt. Surface preparation is directly identified as important: homogeneous, smooth, polished surfaces should provide more representative and accurate results than rough surfaces, where topography, uneven interaction volumes, and shadowing can affect measured intensities. Accelerating voltage controls both sampling depth and X-ray excitation. Lower voltage gives shallower penetration and greater surface sensitivity, while higher voltage probes deeper material and can reduce surface detail. The voltage must exceed the relevant critical ionization energy, with efficient excitation requiring approximately E0 > 2EC. Thus, 5–20 kV should be selected according to the alloying elements and desired sampling depth: too low a voltage may fail to excite characteristic lines, while higher voltage may increase subsurface contributions and reduce surface specificity. The excerpt also notes that quantitative EDS requires appropriate standards.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides useful qualitative guidance for EDS accuracy in aluminum alloys, especially regarding surface condition and measurement intensity. Rough or poorly prepared surfaces can preferentially suppress low-energy X-rays, biasing the analysis; polished, flat specimens generally avoid these geometry-related problems, although areas near sample edges can still obstruct detector line-of-sight paths or cause re-absorption. Incorrect geometry may produce unusually low counts per second or an apparent absence of low-energy peaks. Conductive coatings must be applied uniformly to standards and unknowns, since coating thickness differences can alter measured intensities through absorption of emitted soft X-rays and energy loss of the incident electrons. The excerpt does not give a quantitative relationship between total counts, counting time, count statistics, and EDS accuracy, nor does it specifically compare accelerating voltages from 5 to 20 kV. It does, however, illustrate calculations at 15 kV and notes that primary-electron energy loss becomes especially important when overvoltage is only about 1.5–2; this implies that voltage selection can affect calculated X-ray generation, particularly for lines near their excitation threshold. Matrix corrections are nonlinear and can be seriously wrong for heterogeneous alloys.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific guidance from NIST DTSA-II software, nor does it discuss recommended procedures specifically for aluminum alloys. It does, however, describe general standards-based k-ratio/ZAF quantification versus unnormalised standardless analysis. Standards-based analysis uses experimentally measured standards under similar conditions and thereby cancels dependence on beam current, SEM-EDX geometry, and chamber contamination. It requires one standard for each quantified element, with standards chemically similar to the sample; chemically dissimilar standards increase uncertainty in matrix corrections. For the NIST S479a metallic alloy, pure-element standards were readily available, and the reported standards-based method achieved relative errors below 1% relative to the NIST EDX composition, although ZAF-related uncertainty remained when compared with wet-chemical analysis. Standardless analysis can provide useful results for the alloy, with absolute errors below 2 wt% and relative errors below 3%, but it is described as more conservative and as potentially obscuring uncertainty when normalization is used. The excerpt therefore supports broad guidance favoring chemically matched standards for alloys, but it cannot establish DTSA-II-specific settings or aluminum-alloy recommendations.

contexts.context: The excerpt primarily supports standards-based k-ratio quantification with NIST DTSA-II rather than providing a direct comparison of DTSA-II’s standards-based and standardless workflows. It states that accurate SEM/SDD-EDS analysis requires rigorous EPMA/WDS-style measurement control: highly polished, unetched specimens; identical and reproducible beam energy, dose, detector geometry, tilt, and EDS settings for unknowns and standards; and, for a rigorous k-ratio protocol, beam-current measurement with a Faraday cup and picoammeter. A conservative beam current producing approximately 10% detector deadtime is recommended to reduce coincidence peaks. SDD stability permits use of archived standard spectra, provided quality assurance confirms that current conditions match those used to acquire the standards. Separate mounts containing pure elements and stoichiometric compounds are typical, while alloys may be used if their composition is accurately known and micrometer-scale homogeneity is verified. The excerpt does not give specific DTSA-II guidance on when to choose standardless quantification, nor does it state dedicated recommended procedures for aluminum alloys; it only mentions Al as an example of a pure-element standard and as a source of coincidence peaks at higher deadtime.

contexts.context: The excerpt is a 2018 Goldstein et al. chapter describing rigorous bulk SEM/EDS quantification using NIST DTSA-II’s k-ratio/matrix-correction protocol, but it provides no aluminum-alloy accuracy data or relative errors. It requires homogeneous specimens and identical specimen/standard conditions (beam energy, dose, detector geometry, calibration, dead-time correction, orientation, take-off angle). Surfaces should be highly polished, preferably below 100 nm rms (below 50 nm for sub-1-keV elements); chemical polishing may alter near-surface composition, while ion milling can cause implantation and differential sputtering. Recommended spectra use 5-eV channels and adequate energy span.
contexts.question: Context: we are calibrating quantitative SEM-EDS (Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM, silicon drift detector, NIST DTSA-II, 5-15 kV) for aluminum alloys. The first material is laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg (nominal ~9-11 wt% Si, 0.2-0.45 wt% Mg): both the feedstock powder and as-built printed parts. Later alloys will be Al-based with Mg, Si, Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Zr, Sn, Li, Sc, Ce and Er (families: Al-Si-Mg-Cu, Al-Zn-Mg-Cu 7xxx-type, Al-Cu-Li, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Zr-Er-Sc). We need independent quantitative compositions ('ground truth') to compare our EDS results against, ideally without running hydrofluoric-acid digestions ourselves. What published quantitative evidence exists on the accuracy of SEM-EDS with silicon drift detectors on aluminum alloys, relative to certified or independently measured compositions? Report numeric relative errors for Mg, Si, Cu, Zn, Fe, Mn and other minor or trace elements (0.1-10 wt%) in Al matrices, and how they depend on standardless versus standards-based quantification (e.g., NIST DTSA-II with pure-element or compound standards), accelerating voltage (5-20 kV), total counts and surface preparation. Include work by Newbury and Ritchie (NIST), microanalysis round robins or interlaboratory comparisons that included Al alloys, EDS vs WDS/EPMA comparisons, and EDS vs XRF, LIBS or spark OES comparisons on specific aluminum alloy samples. Is there any open dataset of EDS spectra (or EDS-quantified results) from aluminum alloys of known composition?

Question: Context: we are calibrating quantitative SEM-EDS (Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM, silicon drift detector, NIST DTSA-II, 5-15 kV) for aluminum alloys. The first material is laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg (nominal ~9-11 wt% Si, 0.2-0.45 wt% Mg): both the feedstock powder and as-built printed parts. Later alloys will be Al-based with Mg, Si, Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Zr, Sn, Li, Sc, Ce and Er (families: Al-Si-Mg-Cu, Al-Zn-Mg-Cu 7xxx-type, Al-Cu-Li, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Zr-Er-Sc). We need independent quantitative compositions ('ground truth') to compare our EDS results against, ideally without running hydrofluoric-acid digestions ourselves. What published quantitative evidence exists on the accuracy of SEM-EDS with silicon drift detectors on aluminum alloys, relative to certified or independently measured compositions? Report numeric relative errors for Mg, Si, Cu, Zn, Fe, Mn and other minor or trace elements (0.1-10 wt%) in Al matrices, and how they depend on standardless versus standards-based quantification (e.g., NIST DTSA-II with pure-element or compound standards), accelerating voltage (5-20 kV), total counts and surface preparation. Include work by Newbury and Ritchie (NIST), microanalysis round robins or interlaboratory comparisons that included Al alloys, EDS vs WDS/EPMA comparisons, and EDS vs XRF, LIBS or spark OES comparisons on specific aluminum alloy samples. Is there any open dataset of EDS spectra (or EDS-quantified results) from aluminum alloys of known composition?

## Published Quantitative Evidence on SEM-EDS Accuracy for Aluminum Alloys

### Overview of Available Evidence

Published quantitative evidence on the accuracy of SEM-EDS with silicon drift detectors (SDDs) for aluminum alloys is limited in terms of aluminum-specific benchmarks, but substantial general guidance exists from NIST researchers Newbury and Ritchie, interlaboratory comparisons on related alloys, and multi-technique validation studies.

### General Accuracy Targets from Newbury & Ritchie (NIST)

Newbury and Ritchie have established performance benchmarks for SDD-EDS through extensive validation studies on certified reference materials, stoichiometric compounds, and independently characterized materials (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2). Their 2015 landmark study demonstrated that modern SDD-EDS can achieve accuracy equivalent to wavelength-dispersive spectrometry when following rigorous standards-based k-ratio protocols with proper matrix corrections (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25). The achievable accuracy targets are concentration-dependent: major constituents (>10 wt%) can routinely achieve ±5% relative error, minor constituents (1-10 wt%) approximately ±10% relative error, and trace constituents (0.1-1 wt%) approximately ±25% relative error (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

Their 2024 low-beam-energy study at 5 keV analyzed 263 concentration measurements across 39 elements in 113 materials using NIST DTSA-II software with standards-based k-ratio quantification (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3). More than 98% of results fell within ±5% relative deviation from expected value (RDEV), and 82% were within −2% to +2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). For conventional beam energies (≥10 kV), 122 elemental analyses showed all results within ±5% RDEV and 89% within −2% to +2% RDEV (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22). These figures represent aggregate performance across diverse materials rather than aluminum-alloy-specific results, but they establish achievable accuracy benchmarks for properly conducted SDD-EDS analysis.

### Interlaboratory Comparisons and Round Robin Studies

An interlaboratory comparison by Jonnard et al. (2015) on a nickel-based metallic glass provides insight into EDS versus WDS performance and interlaboratory variability, though not specific to aluminum matrices (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13, jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). At 15-20 kV, EDS analyses from 57 spectrometers across multiple laboratories showed relative standard deviations of 1.06% for Cr (10.5 wt%), 1.43% for Fe (5.4 wt%), 0.77% for Co (23.5 wt%), 0.40% for Ni (51.4 wt%), and 1.94% for Mo (7.1 wt%) (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13). Mean signed errors relative to reference values were +22% for B, +1% for Cr, −4% for Fe, +0.4% for Co, +2% for Ni, and +6% for Mo (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). WDS showed generally lower dispersion: relative standard deviations of 0.48-1.04% versus 0.40-1.94% for EDS (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13).

At 5 kV, EDS precision degraded substantially, with larger dispersions and mean signed errors of −14% for B, +1% for Cr, −30% for Fe, −3% for Co, +7% for Ni, and −10% for Mo (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). The study demonstrated that low-voltage analyses are more challenging and that WDS generally provides better precision than EDS, though careful EDS implementation can approach WDS performance (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13).

### EDS vs. Alternative Techniques on Aluminum Alloys

Seidel et al. (2021) conducted a comprehensive comparison of EDXRF, WDXRF, LIBS, and spark-OES on commercial aluminum alloys, using spark-OES as the benchmark technique (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 7-8, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 2-4). This study, while not focused on SEM-EDS specifically, provides valuable quantitative data on aluminum alloy analysis accuracy. Three certified aluminum alloy reference materials (EB 313, BAM-311, and EB 315a) were analyzed by spark-OES against certified values (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7).

For EB 315a (an Al-Si-Cu alloy with approximately 9.88 wt% Si, closest to AlSi10Mg among the tested materials), spark-OES showed relative deviations of +1.4% for Si, −0.7% for Fe, +2.7% for Cu, +0.6% for Mn, and +7.5% for Mg compared to certified values (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7). Across the three certified aluminum alloys, spark-OES relative errors were generally below 5% for elements at 1-10 wt% concentration and mostly below 10% for elements below 1 wt% (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7).

For light elements critical to aluminum alloys (Mg, Al, Si), LIBS performed better than XRF techniques due to XRF's lower sensitivity for low-Z elements and absorption by air and detector windows (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). A notable exception was EDXRF measurement of Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7, which showed approximately 2 wt% (about 40% relative) deviation above spark-OES values (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). For most major and minor elements, absolute deviations were below 1 wt% for main components and below 0.25 wt% for minor elements below 2 wt% (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10).

### Standards-Based vs. Standardless Quantification

Newbury and Ritchie strongly recommend standards-based k-ratio protocols over standardless quantification for accurate aluminum alloy analysis (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Standardless normalization (where results are internally normalized to 100%) can conceal analytical problems, particularly specimen topography effects and unmeasured constituents (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6). The standards-based k-ratio method requires measuring standards and unknowns under identical conditions (beam energy, dose, EDS parameters, target orientation, and take-off angle) and applying matrix corrections through software such as NIST DTSA-II (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

For aluminum alloys, suitable standards include pure Al, Si, Mg, Cu, Fe, Mn, and other relevant elements, or stoichiometric compounds for reactive/problematic elements (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). While probably more than 98% of reported EDS analyses use standardless methods, achieving WDS-equivalent accuracy requires the k-ratio/standards protocol with polished standards and unknowns plus rigorous matrix corrections (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

### Effect of Accelerating Voltage

Accelerating voltage significantly affects both spatial resolution and analytical accuracy. Newbury and Ritchie's 5 keV study demonstrated that low beam energy is particularly vulnerable to surface contamination and oxidation effects (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). At 5 keV, surface contamination layers (carbon, oxygen) make the analyzed volume a composite of underlying alloy and surface film, potentially causing significant errors (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). Proper materialographic preparation (mounting, grinding, polishing to <100 nm RMS roughness) is essential, especially for low-energy analysis (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

The 5 kV results from Jonnard et al.'s round robin showed substantially poorer precision and larger systematic errors compared to 15-20 kV measurements (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8). For aluminum alloys, 10-20 kV generally provides greater robustness if the relevant X-ray lines (Mg Kα at 1.25 keV, Al Kα at 1.49 keV, Si Kα at 1.74 keV, Cu Kα at 8.05 keV, etc.) remain suitable (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). The beam energy must exceed the critical ionization energy, with efficient excitation requiring E₀ > 2Ec (kallio2025accuracyandprecision pages 15-20, kallio2025accuracyandprecisiona pages 15-20).

### Effect of Count Statistics and Total Counts

Count statistics follow Poisson/Gaussian behavior: one-sigma precision is approximately 3.1% at 1,000 counts, 1.0% at 10,000 counts, 0.31% at 100,000 counts, and 0.10% at 1,000,000 counts (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). These figures describe random uncertainty only; systematic errors from matrix corrections, surface geometry, or detector efficiency remain even with high count totals (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). For trace elements and achieving sub-1000 ppm detection limits, Newbury and Ritchie recommend measurement times of 500 seconds or more to accumulate sufficient counts (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

Higher total counts improve precision but do not eliminate systematic errors from improper surface preparation or unsuitable quantification methods (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 26-29, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 15-20, donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). The tradeoff among accelerating voltage, beam current, and acquisition time affects both count statistics and specimen damage/heating (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 26-29).

### Effect of Surface Preparation

Surface condition is critical for accurate aluminum alloy analysis. Rough, scratched, pitted, or oxidized surfaces can substantially alter electron scattering, X-ray generation, and X-ray absorption paths (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6). Newbury and Ritchie emphasize that a flat, highly polished surface below 100 nm RMS roughness is preferable, with <50 nm RMS recommended when analyzing low-energy photons below 1 keV (C, N, O, F, and low-energy L-lines) (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Rough or irregular surfaces produce geometry-related errors that standardless normalization conceals but that remain problematic for standards-based quantification (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6).

Surface oxidation is especially problematic for aluminum alloys at low beam energy, where even thin oxide layers significantly affect the analyzed composition (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). Chemical polishing should be avoided due to potential shallow compositional changes; physical grinding and polishing with fine abrasives (100 nm diamond, alumina, or ceria) are preferred (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Ion beam milling can be used but may implant ions or cause differential sputtering (goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4). Conductive coatings must be applied uniformly to standards and unknowns since thickness differences alter measured intensities (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 29-34).

### Certified Aluminum Alloy Reference Materials

Several certified reference materials (CRMs) suitable for aluminum alloy calibration have been identified, though availability and current certification status should be confirmed with the issuing institutions:

**NIST SRMs**: SRM 85B and SRM 87A are matrix-matched aluminum-base alloy reference materials for Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Mg, Mn, and Cr (yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 3-6). SRM 1258-I and SRM 1259 are Al-alloy spectrometric reference materials used for XRF and atomic emission calibration (yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 3-6). Microscopic homogeneity must be verified before using bulk spectrometric standards for microanalysis applications. Certified compositions should be obtained from current NIST certificates.

**National Institute of Standards, Egypt**: NIS-CRM067 (Si 0.77, Mg 0.71, Cu 2.40, Zn 2.23, Fe 1.56, Mn 0.40 wt%), NIS-CRM068 (Si 0.49, Mg 0.015, Cu 0.59, Zn 0.030, Fe 0.58, Mn 0.84 wt%), and NIS-CRM069 (Si 0.043, Mg 2.17, Cu 1.55, Zn 5.30, Fe 0.12, Mn 0.083 wt%) provide coverage across multiple aluminum alloy families including 7xxx-type compositions (yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 7-9).

**European CRMs**: EB 313 (Al 94.73, Si 0.36, Mg 3.40, Cu 0.093, Fe 0.39, Mn 0.50 wt%), BAM-311 (Al 91.86, Si 0.20, Mg 1.57, Cu 4.65, Fe 0.31, Mn 0.69 wt%), and EB 315a (Al 85.04, Si 9.88, Mg 0.45, Cu 2.46, Fe 0.62, Mn 0.31 wt%) are commercially available certified aluminum alloy references (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7). EB 315a is the closest available CRM to AlSi10Mg composition, though it contains higher Cu and lower Mg than typical AlSi10Mg.

### Specific Findings for Aluminum Alloy Elements

**Magnesium (Mg)**: Light-element analysis (Z=12) is challenging for X-ray fluorescence techniques due to absorption. LIBS performs better than EDXRF or WDXRF for Mg in aluminum matrices (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). One EDXRF measurement showed approximately +40% relative error for Mg in AlMg4.5Mn0.7 (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 10-13, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). For SEM-EDS at conventional beam energies, Mg Kα (1.25 keV) is readily excited and detected, but surface oxidation can affect results (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18).

**Silicon (Si)**: Silicon analysis shows element-specific challenges across techniques. LIBS agreed better with spark-OES for Si in aluminum alloys than either EDXRF or WDXRF (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 8-10). For EB 315a with 9.88 wt% Si, spark-OES showed +1.4% relative deviation from certified value (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7). Si Kα (1.74 keV) is readily analyzed by SDD-EDS at 5-20 kV.

**Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn), Iron (Fe), and Manganese (Mn)**: These transition metals showed generally good accuracy across multiple techniques. Spark-OES deviations from certified values for Cu, Fe, and Mn in certified aluminum alloys were typically below 5-10% relative for concentrations above 0.1 wt% (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 7-8). The Jonnard et al. round robin on a Ni-based alloy (not aluminum) showed EDS relative standard deviations of 1.4% for Fe and interlaboratory mean errors of −4% at 15-20 kV (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13, jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8).

### Open Datasets and Public Data Availability

No dedicated open-access database of EDS spectra from aluminum alloys of certified composition was identified in the published literature. Newbury and Ritchie (2024) mentioned a publicly supported measurement database associated with their study, containing detector configurations, calibration spectra, analyzed material spectra, standard spectra, and Excel files with raw, normalized, and atomic concentrations plus uncertainty budgets (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18). However, the excerpt did not provide a public download location or confirm aluminum-alloy coverage.

The NIST DTSA-II software and source code are publicly available (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 1-3, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4), providing the quantification engine used in the Newbury and Ritchie studies. This software implements standards-based k-ratio protocols with comprehensive matrix corrections and uncertainty budgets, making it valuable for reproducing and validating quantitative aluminum alloy measurements even in the absence of a dedicated spectral database (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

### Recommendations for AlSi10Mg Calibration

For calibrating quantitative SEM-EDS on LPBF AlSi10Mg powder and printed parts:

1. **Standards-based protocol**: Use pure Al, Si, and Mg metal standards, or suitable compounds for elements difficult to handle in pure form. Measure k-ratios following the protocol described by Goldstein et al. and Newbury & Ritchie, implementing NIST DTSA-II for matrix corrections (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25, newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 1-2, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

2. **Certified reference materials**: EB 315a (9.88 wt% Si, 0.45 wt% Mg, 2.46 wt% Cu) is the closest available CRM to AlSi10Mg, though Cu content differs. NIS-CRM067, NIS-CRM068, NIS-CRM069, or NIST SRM 85B/87A may provide suitable matrix-matched materials for method validation (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 7-9, yamani2021preparationandcertification pages 3-6).

3. **Surface preparation**: Polish samples to <100 nm RMS roughness using physical abrasives. Avoid chemical polishing. For LPBF powder, embedding and polishing cross-sections is preferable to analyzing irregular particle surfaces (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 5-6, goldstein2018quantitativeanalysisthe pages 1-4).

4. **Beam energy**: Use 15 or 20 kV for robust analysis of Al, Si, Mg, and typical minor elements (Fe, Mn, Cu). Lower voltages (5-10 kV) improve spatial resolution but increase vulnerability to surface contamination (newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 18-22, jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 4-8, newbury2024testingtheaccuracy pages 16-18).

5. **Count statistics**: Acquire sufficient counts for desired precision: 10,000+ counts for 1% precision on major peaks, 100,000+ for 0.3% precision (donovan2014electronprobemicroanalysis pages 20-23). For minor elements (0.2-0.5 wt% Mg), 500-second or longer acquisition times may be needed (newbury2015performingelementalmicroanalysis pages 23-25).

6. **Independent validation**: Compare SEM-EDS results against spark-OES, LIBS, or ICP-OES measurements on the same samples. Spark-OES typically achieves <10% relative error for elements >0.1 wt% in aluminum alloys (seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 5-7, seidel2021comparisonofelemental pages 7-8). Alternatively, WDS/EPMA provides higher-precision independent measurements for validation (jonnard2015interlaboratorycomparisonof pages 11-13).

### Limitations and Gaps in Published Evidence

The published literature contains limited aluminum-alloy-specific quantitative SEM-EDS validation data, particularly for:
- LPBF AlSi10Mg and other additive manufacturing aluminum alloys
- 7xxx-series, Al-Cu-Li, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Zr-Er-Sc, and other specialized alloy families mentioned
- Direct element-by-element EDS accuracy benchmarks for Mg, Si, Cu, Zn, Fe, and Mn in aluminum matrices versus certified compositions
- Open-access EDS spectral databases from certified aluminum alloys

Most quantitative evidence comes from general SDD-EDS validation studies (not aluminum-specific) or comparisons using alternative techniques (XRF, LIBS, spark-OES) rather than SEM-EDS directly. The interlaboratory round robins identified involved Ni-based metallic glass rather than aluminum alloys. These gaps suggest opportunities for future work to establish rigorous aluminum-alloy-specific EDS benchmarks, particularly for the alloy families relevant to additive manufacturing and advanced aerospace/automotive applications.

info.query: Context: we are calibrating quantitative SEM-EDS (Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM, silicon drift detector, NIST DTSA-II, 5-15 kV) for aluminum alloys. The first material is laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) AlSi10Mg (nominal ~9-11 wt% Si, 0.2-0.45 wt% Mg): both the feedstock powder and as-built printed parts. Later alloys will be Al-based with Mg, Si, Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Zr, Sn, Li, Sc, Ce and Er (families: Al-Si-Mg-Cu, Al-Zn-Mg-Cu 7xxx-type, Al-Cu-Li, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, Al-Ce-Mg, Al-Zr-Er-Sc). We need independent quantitative compositions ('ground truth') to compare our EDS results against, ideally without running hydrofluoric-acid digestions ourselves. What published quantitative evidence exists on the accuracy of SEM-EDS with silicon drift detectors on aluminum alloys, relative to certified or independently measured compositions? Report numeric relative errors for Mg, Si, Cu, Zn, Fe, Mn and other minor or trace elements (0.1-10 wt%) in Al matrices, and how they depend on standardless versus standards-based quantification (e.g., NIST DTSA-II with pure-element or compound standards), accelerating voltage (5-20 kV), total counts and surface preparation. Include work by Newbury and Ritchie (NIST), microanalysis round robins or interlaboratory comparisons that included Al alloys, EDS vs WDS/EPMA comparisons, and EDS vs XRF, LIBS or spark OES comparisons on specific aluminum alloy samples. Is there any open dataset of EDS spectra (or EDS-quantified results) from aluminum alloys of known composition?
